passages.title: Flux Through a Surface
passages.caption: A constant vector field meets a planar patch with a chosen unit normal. The normal component determines the signed flux through the patch.

source.ref: Equations 3.9–3.12, printed page 3-3 (PDF45); Figure 3-3, printed page 3-2 (PDF44).
source.text: For a surface element, the relevant component of a vector is its component perpendicular to the surface: C · n. A constant planar patch of area A therefore has signed flux (C · n)A. With C=(q,q/2,0) and n=(cos θ,sin θ,0), the illustrated flux is qA(cos θ+(1/2)sin θ). A tangential component makes no contribution. Reversing the normal reverses the sign. For a general surface, the contributions from all surface elements are summed by the surface integral ∫S C · n da. The source calls this surface integral the flux of the vector, even when the vector does not represent a physical flow.
source.limit: The controllable field and planar constant patch are an explicit illustration of the source definition. The patch has uniform area A, the field is constant on it, and n is a unit normal in the xy-plane. Field and normal arrows use separate visual scales. This concept does not model a whole closed-surface net result, heat conservation, a heat source, conductivity, temperature, or an electric-charge law.

passages.title: The flux from a cube; Gauss’ theorem
passages.caption: An axis-aligned cube shows the six faces and their signed outward normals. Add the outward fluxes through each opposite pair of faces.

source.text: For the two faces normal to the x-axis, the outward signs are opposite. The source evaluates each face from the normal component of C, expands C_x across the small x-displacement, and obtains a paired flux proportional to ∂C_x/∂x times the cube volume. The same reasoning for the y- and z-face pairs gives the other two partial derivatives. Their sum is ∇·C, so the outward flux from an infinitesimal cube is (∇·C)ΔV. Subdivision then gives Gauss’ theorem: the flux through a closed surface equals the volume integral of the divergence. The interactive example uses the authored affine field C=(1+lambda*x-omega*y, 0.5+omega*x+lambda*y, 0.25+lambda*z) on a centered cube of side h. Its divergence is 3lambda, and its exact total outward flux is 3lambda*h^3. Because the field is affine, the integral on each face equals its area times the normal component at the face center. For this centered cube, omega changes the underlying field, but symmetry makes each of the six integrated face fluxes, and therefore the net flux, independent of omega. A zero net flux does not require every face flux to be zero.
source.limit: The source argument uses a small axis-aligned cube and neglects higher-order terms in the infinitesimal limit for a general smooth field. The displayed finite equality is exact only for the authored affine field. The controls use h for cube side, lambda for expansion, and omega for rotation. Signed outward normals are used on all six faces. This is a vector-flux and divergence model, not an electrostatic charge law or a material-flow animation.

passages.title: Count each interaction once
passages.caption: Uniform volume-charge example · cumulative rho-phi energy · R/a

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · 8-5 · source formulas with an authored radial example
source.text:
Replace each small charge by ρ dV. Integrating both labels gives U = ½∫∫ Kρ₁ρ₂/|r₁−r₂| dV₁dV₂: each pair occurs in the two orders. The inner integral is φ(r₁), so U = ½∫ρφ dV. For two ideal point charges, φ₁ means the potential of charge 2 only and φ₂ the potential of charge 1 only. Both q₁φ₁ and q₂φ₂ equal the same mutual energy; their half-sum counts it once. A point’s own potential is excluded from that mutual formula.

The visual checks a regular, uniformly charged volume ball with radius a>0 and fixed charge Q>0, with φ→0 at infinity. Move R/a to include successive regions. Inside the ball, ρ is constant and φ = (KQ/2a)[3−(r/a)²]; outside, ρ=0. The cumulative half-ρφ integral reaches 3Ea/5 at R=a, where Ea=KQ²/a, and stays there. The continuous distribution includes work between its subelements, including assembly of what becomes one finite charge. This differs from subtracting each ideal point’s self contribution. The labelled field-energy comparison belongs to this same regular example; it is not an integral solver for arbitrary densities.
source.limit: Regular authored uniform volume ball; normalized energy scale Ea=KQ²/a. Source general integrals and pair bookkeeping are explained; the slider evaluates one specialization. No point-self subtraction, nuclear model, or charge dynamics.

passages.title: A total does not locate energy
passages.caption: Source argument map · select a claim · arrows show reasoning

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · 8-5 · source argument, original paraphrase
source.text:
A conserved total says that losses and gains balance overall. By itself it does not locate the energy or require anything to pass between the places where the changes occur. Local accounting adds a stronger condition: a region’s energy change must be accounted for by transfer through its boundary. The map separates the total, the regional balance, and that transfer requirement. Selecting a claim highlights its logical role; the arrows describe reasons and qualifications, not energy trajectories.

The passage says nature does conserve energy locally; that physical claim is distinct from what a conserved total alone establishes. The passage also motivates location through mass-energy equivalence, E=mc², and gravity’s response to mass. That relation is symbolic context here; this aid computes no mass, gravity, rate, or propagation. The source then preserves a caveat: electrostatics alone does not determine where energy is located. Full electrodynamics gives more information, while the localization remains not strictly unique. The following static field-energy representation is a useful account of the total, but its equality alone supplies no local transport law.
source.limit: Qualitative source argument. Claim selection is authored navigation, not time or a physical variable. E=mc² is dimension-checked, noncomputed source context. No gravitational calculation or electromagnetic transport model.

passages.title: Include the exterior field
passages.caption: Regular radial example · finite integral plus remaining outer tail

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · 8-5 · source formulas with an authored radial example
source.text:
For vacuum electrostatics, Eq.8.30 gives U = (ε₀/2)∫all space |E|² dV, numerically equal to the charge-potential total under the conditions explained next. All space includes regions outside the charges. The radiation analogy motivates assigning energy to fields, but this static electric formula does not describe a traveling wave’s full electric-plus-magnetic energy or its transport.

Our authored example is a uniform volume-charge ball, radius a>0 and fixed charge Q>0. The radial field grows linearly inside and falls as 1/r² outside. The local integrand varies with radius; a spherical shell adds (ε₀/2)|E|² 4πr²dr. The graph and cumulative integral use that physical volume weighting. In units Ea=KQ²/a, the total is 3/5. Only 1/10 lies inside r=a; the remaining 1/2 lies outside. A finite R includes less than the total: for R≥a, Ufield(<R)/Ea=3/5−a/(2R). The tail a/(2R) is displayed separately. Move R/a and check that the two contributions still sum to 3/5.

This passage covers the global representation. The next retained aid explains Eq.8.31’s local energy per physical volume. The separate Fig.8-8 sidebar is reviewed as auxiliary source context, outside this new gap’s bounds.

passages.title: Pair interaction energy and a many-charge sum
passages.caption: Original bounded experiment · source and supplied inputs labeled

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · source-bound original prepared explanation
source.text:
Bring each point charge from infinity into the potential produced by charges already present. Every unordered pair contributes K qi qj/rij once. Reversing the assembly order changes the intermediate work but leaves the final mutual energy unchanged. The authored three-site example is planar within three-dimensional vacuum; its signed charges and separations are supplied inputs. It excludes each ideal point’s own potential. The directed sum over qi times the potential from all other sites counts each pair twice, so its half gives total mutual energy. Fig 8-1 supplies the two-charge separation context.

For a continuous density, divide space into small cells and replace each cell charge by rho times its volume. In the limit the corresponding sums become integrals: U=one half times the integral of rho phi over space (later Eq 8.28, separately reviewed context). That smooth-distribution assembly definition is distinct from excluding ideal point self terms. The source’s density-integral transition is explained here; the finite three-site experiment does not numerically solve an arbitrary continuous distribution.

passages.title: Assembling a uniformly charged solid sphere
passages.caption: Original bounded experiment · source and supplied inputs labeled

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · source-bound original prepared explanation
source.text:
Assemble a prescribed uniform volume density in concentric thin layers brought quasistatically from infinity. At radius r, the already assembled charge Qr produces boundary potential KQr/r; adding dQ needs dU=KQr dQ/r (Eq 8.4). Fig 8-2 distinguishes the growing radius r, thin increment dr and final radius a. Uniform density gives Qr=4πrho r³/3 and dQ=4πrho r²dr. Substitution gives dU=4πrho²r⁴dr/(3epsilon 0), whose integral from 0 to a is U=4πrho²a⁵/(15epsilon 0). With Q=4πrho a³/3 this equals 3 KQ²/(5 a).

The slider follows the same fixed-density path: at x=r/a, enclosed charge is Qx³ and work is U(a)x⁵. Changing the final charge or radius selects a different prescribed density. It is not compression of a fixed charge. Zero charge gives zero work. The charge and density forms of final work are shown independently. Comparing continuous pair energy U=(1/2)KQ² times the mean inverse separation with the final result gives mean(1/r 12)=6/(5 a). That geometric average refers to the final uniform ball and remains finite at zero charge; no division by zero is performed. Ideal point self-energy and conducting-shell energy have different definitions.

passages.caption: Original bounded experiment · source and supplied inputs labeled

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · source-bound original prepared explanation
source.text:
Transfer charge quasistatically between the capacitor’s conductors. For fixed positive linear capacitance C, the instantaneous voltage is V=q/C (Eq 8.8), so the next small increment needs work V dq. Integrating this rising voltage from zero to the selected q gives q²/(2 C), rather than using the final voltage for every increment. The triangle under the physical charge–voltage line is that work: pC times volts gives pJ.

At the selected state, V=q/C, hence U=q²/(2 C)=CV²/2 (Eqs 8.9 and 8.10). These are two forms of the same energy. Charging fraction changes q while C stays fixed; the capacitance slider chooses a different charging case. At zero final charge, voltage and work are zero, while the ratio to final work is undefined. This aid concerns quasistatic charge transfer in a linear capacitor; the subsequent conducting-sphere and mechanical-work arguments have their own source passages.

passages.title: Force from a supplied capacitance curve
passages.caption: Fixed Q · external force = dU/dx · electrical force is opposite

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · 8-2 · original source explanation and supplied-input experiment
source.text:
Keep the capacitor disconnected so Q stays fixed. Its stored energy is U=Q²/(2 C). A quasistatic external displacement supplies mechanical work equal to dU. For positive coordinate x, Fext dx=dU=(Q²/2)d(1/C), so Fext=−Q² C′(x)/(2 C²). The balancing external force and the electrical force have opposite signs. This avoids resolving every surface charge when the dependence C(x) is already known.

The diagram supplies three original positive analytic inputs: c(s)=1/s, 1+s or exp(s), with s=x/L, L=1 mm, C=C 0 c, C 0=100 pF and Q=20 nC. These are examples, not capacitances inferred from the sketch. Stored energy has scale E 0=2 microjoule; force has scale E 0/L=2 millinewton. The derivative of C uses physical metres, while the slider shows x/L. Decreasing capacitance raises energy at fixed Q; increasing it lowers energy.

The differential result applies to an infinitesimal displacement at the selected point. A finite change requires integrating the force, equivalently subtracting the endpoint energies. Multiplying one frozen derivative by a large change in capacitance is generally incorrect. The source’s general virtual-work reasoning remains broader than these three supplied curves.

passages.title: Torque from a supplied angular capacitance
passages.caption: Fixed Q · angular derivative uses radians · C(θ) is authored

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · 8-2 · original source explanation and supplied-input experiment
source.text:
The same fixed-charge virtual-work reasoning works for any displacement component. Choose the corresponding component of the external force and the small displacement in that direction. For a pivoted electrode, use angular work: τ_ext dθ=dU. Thus τ_ext=−Q²(dC/dθ)/(2 C²), and electrical torque is its opposite. The capacitance change must correspond to that same angular displacement.

Fig 8-3 depicts interleaved rotating capacitor electrodes at two potentials. It motivates this angular coordinate but supplies no numerical C(θ) law. The diagram therefore uses an explicitly authored positive input C=C 0[1+0.4 cos(θ)], fixed Q=20 nC and C 0=100 pF. The abstract arm indicates angle and is not a computed electrode-overlap or fringing-field model.

The slider uses degrees for reading. It converts them to radians before evaluating derivatives; torque is energy per radian, in N·m. A derivative per degree must be converted and must not be labelled N·m directly. At 60 degrees, C/C 0=6/5, U/E 0=5/6 and τ_ext/E 0=5 sqrt(3)/36. The electrical tendency lowers energy; the balancing external torque raises it. Finite angular work is the endpoint energy difference, rather than a fixed torque times an arbitrary large turn.

passages.title: Pair double counting versus energy per NaCl molecule
passages.caption: Original bounded experiment · source and supplied inputs labeled

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · source-bound original prepared explanation
source.text:
Let S be the interaction of one ion with every other ion, excluding itself. In an ideal bulk lattice with equivalent ions, summing these one-ion contributions counts each shared pair twice. The assigned energy per ion is therefore S/2. One NaCl formula unit contains two ions, so its Coulomb contribution is 2(S/2)=S. Counting N equivalent bulk formula units gives total NS; its directed sum is 2 NS. Negative binding contribution and positive separation-work magnitude have opposite signs.

The source uses e² as shorthand for Kqe², where qe is the elementary charge and K=1/(4πepsilon 0). At the source nearest-ion spacing, e²/a is about 5.12 eV. The default S=−10eV is an explicitly supplied counting example, not a computed NaCl lattice sum or measured complete binding energy. Controls rescale this negative input and the equivalent bulk amount. The two drawn ions are representatives of the all-other-ion sum; they do not form an isolated pair. A finite cluster generally has inequivalent boundary ions, so the bulk per-ion argument cannot be transferred to it without a separate calculation.

passages.caption: Original bounded experiment · source and supplied inputs labeled

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · source-bound original prepared explanation
source.text:
After the central alternating line, consider one adjacent parallel line. Its nearest opposite ion is at a; successive symmetric pairs are at sqrt(1+j²)a with alternating signs. The supplied scale Kqe²/a is 5.12eV. Including N pairs gives S_N=−1+2 sum[j=1..N](−1)^(j+1)/sqrt(1+j²). The plotted geometry uses the same spacing in both directions. Increasing N changes a finite partial, not an exact infinite answer; consecutive partials bracket that same-line limit and the next term bounds its alternating remainder.

There are four nearest parallel lines, followed by more distant diagonal and other lines. Their properly defined complete three-dimensional Coulomb sum has the separately source-supplied coefficient 1.747. Multiplying it by 5.12eV gives−8.94464eV, while the source prints about−8.94eV. The finite adjacent-line experiment does not derive 1.747. This attraction-only result overstates the observed 7.92eV separation magnitude by roughly thirteen percent with these printed numbers; the source describes the discrepancy approximately as about ten percent. passages.title: Keep the signed boundary term
passages.caption: Finite sphere · Uρφ = Ufield − B · B retains its sign

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · 8-5 · source formulas with an authored radial example
source.text:
Use Poisson’s relation rho=−epsilon 0 Laplacian(phi). The exact product identity is phi Laplacian(phi)=div(phi grad(phi))−|grad(phi)|²; For one component, ∂x(phi ∂xphi)=(∂xphi)²+phi ∂x²phi; summing x,y,z gives the identity and cancels the gradient terms. The product rule separates a divergence from minus the squared potential gradient. The first minus sign therefore leaves a positive field integral and a negative outward surface integral. With B=(epsilon 0/2)∮phi ∂nphi da, the finite-volume relation is Uρphi=Ufield−B. Gauss’s theorem and E=−grad(phi) supply the general proof.

The authored regular ball checks both integrals at the same R. A separate fourth bar shows the field energy outside R: Ufield(all)−Ufield(inside R). For R≥a all charge is enclosed, so this outside field energy equals −B. For R<a it also includes the remaining charge–potential contribution and differs from −B. At R=0 the outside field energy is the full 3Ea/5 even though B=0. Negative B and positive omitted field energy have different meanings.

For localized charge with zero potential at infinity, phi falls as 1/R, its gradient as 1/R², and surface area grows as R²; B falls as 1/R. A neutral localized source falls faster. Only the all-space limit removes the outer boundary term and yields Eq 8.35. Finite boundaries, singular inner boundaries and nonlocalized fields require their own accounting.

passages.title: The divergence is at the origin
passages.caption: Point field · positive excluded radius b · outer radius R=4a

source.ref: Feynman Vol. II · 8-6 · source formulas with an authored radial example
source.text:
The mutual energy of distinct ideal points excludes each point’s own potential. Building an extended distribution instead includes the work of assembling its charge. Shrinking a fixed total charge into an ideal point makes the classical field-energy integral diverge at the origin. This does not arise from the distant field: its outer tail converges.

source.limit: The illustration uses the authored field T = 20 + αx + βy degrees C in a uniform z slice. The controls use x from -1 to 1 m and α and β from -2 to 2 K/m. The default values are x = 0.4 m, α = 2 K/m, and β = 1 K/m. No gradient arrows, heat-flow law, or measured source temperatures are represented. If α and β are both zero, the scalar field is uniform.

passages.title: Velocity in a Rotating Body
passages.caption: A rotating body has a velocity vector at each point. The arrows show instantaneous velocity, not particle paths.

source.text: A vector field assigns a vector to each point, so one rotating body can have different velocity arrows at different positions. In the authored model, v=ω(-y,x,0) m/s. At the probe (x,0,0), the velocity is tangent to the rotation and its speed is |ω x|. Thus, changing position can change both the velocity direction and magnitude. Heat flow h is a different vector field, measured in W/m².
source.limit: The body rotates rigidly and instantaneously about the z-axis. The angular speed ω ranges from -1 to 1 s⁻¹, and the probe coordinate x ranges from -0.9 to 0.9 m. The arrows represent local velocity samples; they are not trajectories. Parameter defaults are illustrative.

passages.title: Heat Flow Through an Oriented Surface Patch
passages.caption: A small planar patch measures the component of heat flow normal to it. Reversing the chosen unit normal reverses the signed heat rate.

source.section: Vector fields: local heat flow through a surface
source.text: Use the authored uniform heat-flux field C=(q,q/2,0) W/m² and the patch normal n=(cos θ,sin θ,0). The normal heat-flux density is C·n=q cos θ+(q/2) sin θ W/m². For actual patch area A, the signed heat rate is (C·n)A W. Reversing n changes its sign. The area A is not a projected area.
source.limit: The patch is small, planar, and has locally uniform heat flow. The field arrow and unit-normal arrow use separate visual scales. This is one constant planar patch, not a whole closed surface. It does not model heat conservation, heat sources, conductivity, temperature, or electric charge.

passages.title: When Three Derivatives Form a Vector
passages.caption: Rotate the coordinate axes while the physical gradient and displacement stay fixed. Their components change, but their lengths and dot product do not.

source.ref: Section 2-3, “Derivatives of fields—the gradient,” equations (2.11) and (2.12), printed page 2-4.
source.text: Three numbers are not sufficient to define a vector. An individual derivative such as ∂T/∂x depends on the chosen axes. The three derivatives qualify as vector components only if they transform together correctly when the axes rotate. An invariant test requires their contraction with every vector to remain the same scalar, not only their contraction with one selected direction.
source.limit: The illustration uses the authored two-dimensional field T=20+2x+y with z=z′ and zero curvature. The physical gradient is (2,1) degrees C/m. The displacement length h ranges from 0.1 to 0.8 m, its physical direction β ranges from 0° to 360°, and the passive axis rotation θ ranges from −90° to 90°. The transformed gradient is g′=(gx cos θ+gy sin θ, −gx sin θ+gy cos θ), and the displacement uses the same transformation. This linear field makes the finite temperature change equal to the dot product exactly; the source passage establishes the vector criterion and invariant-contraction setup, not the later gradient-specific transformation proof.

passages.title: The del operator needs an operand
passages.caption: Apply ∇=(∂/∂x, ∂/∂y, ∂/∂z) to T=20+αx+βy+γz to obtain ∇T=(α,β,γ).

source.text: The scalar-gradient transformation argument does not depend on the particular scalar field. This permits the gradient components to be abstracted into the operator ∇. Its rectangular components are derivative operations, so ∇ alone is not a numerical arrow. It must act on an operand such as T before it produces the vector field ∇T.
source.limit: The bounded illustration uses the authored scalar field T=20+αx+βy+γz degrees C. The controls set x from −1 to 1 m and α, β, and γ from −2 to 2 K/m. The displayed value of x changes T but not this linear field's constant gradient. Parameter defaults are illustrative.

passages.title: Operator Order: T∇ and ∇T
passages.caption: For T=1+αx and f=βx², the display compares (T∇)f with (∇T)f at x. The quantities generally differ because the derivative acts on the expression to its right.

source.text: The symbol ∇ is an operator that needs an operand. Multiplying it on the left by T does not satisfy it: T∇ remains an operator, and (T∇)f means T∇f. In ∇T, T is on the operator’s right, so ∇ differentiates T and produces a vector field. Order matters when T varies with position. For these authored fields, the product rule is: ∇(Tf)=T∇f+f∇T, so T∇f must not be silently replaced by ∇(Tf).
source.limit: This is a dimensionless illustration on R³ with T=1+αx and f=βx², uniform in y and z. The controls are x from −1 to 1 m, α from −1 to 1 m⁻¹, and β from 0.5 to 2 m⁻². Both displayed applied quantities have units m⁻¹. The product-rule comparison is an authored elaboration, not a formula stated in the selected source interval.

passages.title: Gradient and the Steepest Direction
passages.caption: At P, compare the local directional slope with the exact finite change along a displacement of length h.

source.text: The gradient is the spatial rate-of-change vector. Its component along a unit direction is the directional derivative, so the maximizing unit direction is parallel to the gradient. For the authored field T(x,y)=20+2x+y+(κ/2)(x²+y²), the gradient at P=(0,0) is (2,1) °C/m. A displacement at angle β has first-order change h(2 cos β+sin β), while the exact finite change also contains κh²/2. Thus, nonlinear curvature can make a finite change differ from its local linear prediction.
source.limit: This is a two-dimensional slice with fixed z. It illustrates a local scalar-field derivative, not force or heat-flow dynamics. The controls vary h, β, and κ within their stated bounds. If the gradient is zero, every unit direction has zero directional derivative, so no unique steepest direction exists. A negative local slope alone does not guarantee a negative finite change. The numerical field is an authored illustration, not source data or a general exact finite identity.

passages.title: Divergence as a scalar derivative sum
passages.caption: For C=(1+λ x−ω y, 0.5+ω x+λ y, 0.25+λ z), div C=3λ. The displayed arrows are the xy projection, not material trajectories.

source.text: The dot product of ∇ with a vector field produces the scalar divergence. In the derivative matrix, the three contributing entries are ∂Cx/∂x, ∂Cy/∂y, and ∂Cz/∂z—the diagonal entries λ, λ, and λ. Their sum is 3λ m⁻¹. The off-diagonal terms −ω and ω do not contribute. Changing ω changes the field but not its divergence. Under a basis rotation, first express the field in the new coordinates and then differentiate; the resulting divergence is the same scalar.
source.limit: This is a bounded affine, dimensionless field with coordinates measured in meters. The controls use probe coordinate x from −1 to 1 m and λ and ω from −1 to 1 m⁻¹. It illustrates the divergence definition only, not flow, conservation, or a general solver. For the source field h measured in W/m², divergence has units W/m³ instead.

passages.title: Curl from crossed spatial derivatives
passages.caption: In a fixed right-handed basis, the xy arrows show the affine field’s xy projection. At the probe, the display compares ∂C_y/∂x and ∂C_x/∂y and gives the z component of curl.

source.text: The cross product with ∇ produces a vector. For C=(1+λx−ωy, 0.5+ωx+λy, 0.25+λz), the z component is ∂C_y/∂x−∂C_x/∂y=ω−(−ω)=2ω. The other curl components are zero because the required cross-coordinate derivatives are zero. Thus curl C=(0,0,2ω). The arrows are a field projection, not material trajectories. Curl is not material angular velocity itself; for rigid rotation, curl is twice the angular velocity. The source postpones physical interpretation.
source.limit: This is an authored dimensionless affine field with coordinates in meters. The controls vary probe x, expansion λ, and rotation ω. The basis is fixed and right-handed. All z derivatives and unshown cross derivatives that occur in this curl calculation are zero. The diagonal derivative ∂C_z/∂z=λ can be nonzero, but it does not occur in curl.

passages.title: A Vacuum Plane Wave Satisfies Maxwell’s Equations
passages.caption: An exact source-free wave with E along y, B along z, and propagation along +x. The graph compares E_y with the explicitly rescaled quantity cB_z in V/m.

source.text: Let φ=kx−ckt, E=(0,E₀ cos φ,0), and B=(0,0,E₀ cos φ/c). Then ∇×E has z-component −kE₀ sin φ, equal to −∂B/∂t. Also, c²∇×B has y-component ckE₀ sin φ, equal to ∂E/∂t when j=0. Both divergences are zero, so the first and third equations hold with ρ=0. Thus, the spatial and time derivatives satisfy both curl equations with the stated signs. Move the spatial probe to compare both derivatives at the same P and time. The blue E arrow lies along y. The gold dot or cross shows B normal to the page, with fixed glyph size for direction only.
source.limit: This is one exact source-free vacuum plane wave, with ρ=0 and j=0. It is not a general Maxwell solver. The fixed wave number is k=π m⁻¹ and c=299792458 m/s. E is measured in V/m and B in T; only cB is displayed on the rescaled V/m comparison axis. The phase control sets the time at x=0, and the amplitude control changes E₀ throughout its bounded range. Spatial probe x−1..1 m. B glyph is direction only; its tesla magnitude is the numerical readout.

passages.title: Heat conduction through a slab
passages.caption: A homogeneous slab has thickness d and cross-sectional area A. Its left face is at 20 °C, and its right face is at 20 °C + ΔT. The +x direction points from left to right; the fixed-length arrow shows only the direction of heat flow.

source.text: For steady one-dimensional conduction, h_x = −κΔT/d and J_x = h_x A, where J_x is thermal energy per second in W. With κ, A, and the endpoint temperatures fixed, doubling d halves the magnitude of J_x. Its sign stays the same. This conduction law is approximate for applicable materials, not a universal exact law.
source.limit: The slab is homogeneous and isotropic, κ > 0, d > 0, the transverse dimensions are uniform, conduction is steady and one-dimensional, and there is no internal heat generation. The temperature profile applies only for 0 ≤ x ≤ d.

passages.title: Heat flows down the temperature gradient
passages.caption: For T=20+αx+βy, the blue vector is ∇T and the gold vector is h=−κ∇T. For a nonzero gradient, they point in opposite directions. Both vectors vanish when the temperature is uniform.

source.text: A tiny slab is oriented with its faces parallel to the local isotherms. The temperature change per perpendicular distance gives the maximum local rate of change, |∇T|. Heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature, so its direction is opposite to ∇T. Therefore, for scalar conductivity κ, h=−κ∇T. Changing κ changes the heat-flux magnitude, while changing α or β changes the temperature gradient and its direction.
source.limit: The authored field is T=20+αx+βy degrees C, with α and β in K/m and scalar κ in W/(m K). It illustrates local isotropic bulk conduction. The blue gradient and gold heat-flux arrows use separate scales. The isotherms are static. Zero temperature gradient gives zero heat flux. The model does not include anisotropic tensor conductivity, time evolution, diffusion, or material calibration.

passages.title: A nonuniform gradient can have zero curl
passages.caption: For ψ=20+2x+y+ηxy, the gradient varies with position, but its curl is zero.

source.text: The vector mnemonic A×A=0 suggests ∇×(∇ψ)=0, but the component calculation supplies the reason: each curl component is a difference of equal mixed partial derivatives. For the displayed field, ∇ψ=(2+ηy,1+ηx), so the z-component is ∂x(1+ηx)−∂y(2+ηy)=η−η=0; the other components are also zero. Thus a gradient field can be nonuniform and still have zero curl.
source.limit: The authored example is the smooth polynomial ψ=20+2x+y+ηxy degrees C on the displayed domain. Continuous second partial derivatives are required so that mixed partial derivatives are equal. The controls use η from −1 to 1 degrees C/m² and probe x from −1 to 1 m at y=0. This example illustrates the general identity; it is not source numerical data.

passages.title: A curl can be nonzero while its divergence is zero
passages.caption: For C=(0,0,ηxy), curl C=(ηx,−ηy,0), but div(curl C)=η−η+0=0.

source.text: The source first uses A·(A×B)=0 as a mnemonic for ∇·(∇×h)=0, then says that the differential operations can be carried through with components. In the authored example, the curl field is generally nonzero. Its divergence is zero because the component derivatives cancel. This differential identity requires sufficient smoothness for the relevant mixed derivatives to commute; ordinary-vector orthogonality alone is not its proof.
source.limit: Use the bounded smooth polynomial field C=(0,0,ηxy) W/m², with η from −1 to 1 W/m⁴ and probe x from −1 to 1 m at y=0. The display shows curl C in W/m³ and its component derivatives in W/m⁴. The unit-cube outward flux contributions η, −η, and 0 cancel across the three axis pairs. This example does not imply that one zero net flux or one sampled point guarantees a global vector potential.

passages.title: A Potential for a Curl-Free Field
passages.caption: The authored potential ψ=20+2x+y+κ(x²+y²)/2 gives ∇ψ=(2+κx,1+κy,0). Compare the direct path from A=(0,0) to B=(1,1) with the path through (1,0).

source.text: The source states, without proof, that a field with zero curl is the gradient of a scalar field. In this illustration, the displayed field is produced by ψ: taking its gradient gives (2+κx,1+κy,0), whose curl is zero. Exact changes in ψ telescope to the same endpoint difference on either path. The finite left-endpoint sums approach that difference as N increases; agreement for these two paths alone does not prove the general theorem.
source.limit: The polynomial ψ is smooth on all R² and can be extended unchanged in z over R³. Thus, the domain has no excluded holes or singularities. More generally, the converse requires an appropriate smooth domain, such as a simply connected domain with admissible spanning surfaces. The source does not state this qualification and does not prove the theorem. N ranges from 1 to 32, κ from 0 to 1.5 degrees C/m², and the path selector chooses the direct diagonal or the path through (1,0).

passages.title: A vector potential for a divergence-free field
passages.caption: For C=(0,0,-ω(x²+y²)/2), its curl is D=ω(-y,x,0), and div D=0.

source.text: The source states that a field with zero divergence can be written as the curl of a vector field. This illustration gives an explicit example: differentiating C produces the displayed rotating field D. Thus, C is a vector potential for D.
source.limit: The authored fields are smooth on all of R³, which is contractible. The controls vary ω from -1 to 1 m⁻¹ and the probe coordinate x from -1 to 1 m. This is an explicit construction, not a general inverse solver or a proof of the theorem. A general global vector-potential claim needs suitable domain conditions; simple connectedness alone is insufficient. This explicit polynomial construction has no excluded holes or singularities.

passages.title: The Scalar Laplacian
passages.caption: For T=20+H cos(kx), compare the temperature offset T−20 °C with ∇²T=−Hk² cos(kx). The Laplacian is a scalar sum of spatial second partial derivatives.

source.section: Combinations of two ∇ operators; the Laplacian
source.text: Two combinations of ∇ can always give zero, but ∇·(∇T) is not zero in general. Expanding it gives ∂²T/∂x²+∂²T/∂y²+∂²T/∂z², which is the scalar operator ∇², called the Laplacian. In the illustrated field, T varies only with x, so ∇²T=-Hk² cos(kx), which is generally nonzero. This is a second-derivative scalar, not a first directional derivative or a vector.
source.limit: The controlled field T=20+H cos(kx) degrees C is an authored illustration, uniform in y and z. The amplitude H ranges from 0.2 to 5 K, the wave number k ranges from 0.5 to 3 m⁻¹, and the probe coordinate x ranges from -1 to 1 m. The displayed Laplacian has units K/m². This example does not introduce a heat equation.

passages.title: Laplacian of a Vector Field
passages.caption: For h=(0,H cos(kx),0) W/m², the scalar Laplacian acts on each fixed Cartesian component: ∇²h=(0,−Hk² cos(kx),0) W/m⁴.

source.ref: Page 2-10, componentwise vector Laplacian statement following Eq. (2.54).
source.text: In rectangular coordinates, apply the same scalar Laplacian separately to hₓ, hᵧ, and h_z. Here only hᵧ varies, so only the y-component of ∇²h is nonzero.
source.limit: This bounded illustration uses a fixed Cartesian basis and a field that is uniform in y and z. It does not justify applying scalar component formulas unchanged in a varying basis. H, k, and the probe position vary within the template bounds.

passages.title: Curl of a Curl and Operator Order
passages.caption: For the smooth fixed-basis field h=(L cos(kx), H cos(kx), 0), compare grad(div h), the vector Laplacian, and curl(curl h).

source.section: Double del operations: curl of a curl
source.text: Substituting ∇ into the vector triple-product identity requires the differential operators to keep their operands on the right. The expression h(∇·∇) leaves ∇·∇ as an unfinished operator, so it does not produce the required vector field. Reordering the scalar factor gives (∇·∇)h=∇²h and therefore ∇×(∇×h)=∇(∇·h)−∇²h. In the illustration, the longitudinal component cancels between the two right-hand terms, while the transverse component remains. This single smooth field illustrates the component identity; it is not a general proof.
source.limit: The authored field h=(L cos(kx),H cos(kx),0) W/m² is globally smooth and uses a fixed Cartesian basis. The controls vary x from −1 to 1 m, H from 0.2 to 2 W/m², k from 0.5 to 3 m⁻¹, and L from −2 to 2 W/m². Its divergence is −Lk sin(kx) W/m³. Its grad div is (−Lk² cos(kx),0,0) W/m⁴. Its vector Laplacian is (−Lk² cos(kx),−Hk² cos(kx),0) W/m⁴. Subtraction gives curl curl=(0,Hk² cos(kx),0) W/m⁴.

passages.title: Gradient of a divergence
passages.caption: For h=(α x²,β x²,0), divergence first produces the scalar 2α x. Its gradient is (2α,0,0), while the vector Laplacian is (2α,2β,0).

source.ref: Printed page 2-11, paragraph immediately before the table of conclusions.
source.text: The source identifies ∇(∇·h) as a possible vector field with no special universal value. This authored field shows why: ∇(∇·h) can be nonzero and can differ from ∇²h when β is nonzero.
source.limit: Use the smooth authored field h=(α x²,β x²,0) W/m². The probe coordinate x varies from -1 m to 1 m. The controls α and β vary independently from -1 to 1 W/m⁴. The displayed divergence has units W/m³, and the displayed gradient and vector Laplacian have units W/m⁴. This bounded illustration is not a general proof or a claim that grad div equals div grad.

passages.title: Two gradients need not be parallel
passages.caption: The diagram compares ∇ψ=(a,0,0) and ∇φ=(b cos θ,b sin θ,0). Their cross product is (0,0,ab sin θ), so it can be nonzero, but it is zero when the gradients are parallel.

source.text: The same ∇ symbol does not make ∇ψ and ∇φ equal: each gradient acts on a different scalar function. In this illustration, changing θ changes the angle between the two gradients and therefore changes their cross product. This does not conflict with ∇×∇ψ=0, where the curl operator acts on the gradient of one sufficiently smooth scalar field.
source.limit: This is a static illustration with dimensionless scalar fields with ψ=ax and φ=b(x cos θ+y sin θ), where a and b range from 0.5 to 1.5 m^-1 and θ ranges from -180° to 180°. It is not a general editable three-dimensional field or a coordinate-rotation model.

passages.title: A Fixed Vector in a Varying Radial Basis
passages.caption: A constant Cartesian vector V=(1,0) stays fixed while the radial unit vector changes around a circle of radius R>0. At polar angle theta, V_r=cos(theta) and V_theta=-sin(theta).

source.section: Vector differential operators in nonrectangular coordinates
source.ref: Printed page 2-12; Eq. (2.60) and the following discussion of radial components and fixed component directions.
source.text: The radial component changes because “radial” denotes a different direction at each point. For V=(1,0), the vector Laplacian is zero, so its radial projection is zero. However, treating V_r=cos(theta) as a scalar gives ∇²V_r=-cos(theta)/R². Thus, the scalar Laplacian of a varying-basis component is not generally the corresponding component of the vector Laplacian.
source.limit: This is a bounded two-dimensional illustration on the punctured plane with R>0. The vector is constant and dimensionless. The displayed circle is schematic; the radius control changes the physical derivative. The example does not provide a general polar-coordinate formula for the vector Laplacian.

passages.title: From a sampled gradient sum to a line integral
passages.caption: Divide each leg of the directed path from A to B into N segments. Each sampled tangential contribution enters the signed sum. The finite left-endpoint sum approaches the exact endpoint change as N increases.

source.text: The gradient gives the local rate of change of a scalar field. Along a directed path, its dot product with a line element selects the signed tangential component. Marking the path into segments produces a sum of sampled tangential components times segment lengths. The line integral is the limit of this sum as the largest segment length approaches zero; a finite sampled sum is not, in general, the exact integral. The display uses the illustrative field ψ=20+2x+y+κ(x²+y²)/2 on all R², with A=(0,0) and B=(1,1). It compares the direct diagonal with the path through (1,0). For either displayed path, the left-endpoint sum differs from ψ(B)−ψ(A) by κ/N degrees C, while the limiting integral equals the endpoint difference.
source.limit: The authored polynomial ψ=20+2x+y+κ(x²+y²)/2 is smooth on all R². Coordinates are meters; ψ is degrees C. N is 1–32 segments per leg; κ is 0–1.5 °C/m². Choose the direct diagonal or the two-leg path through (1,0), with the same endpoints A=(0,0), B=(1,1). Exact segment changes telescope for every N. Finite left-endpoint gradient samples approach the integral in the limit. The example is original, not source numerical data. This unit stops before the proof of Eq. (3.1).

passages.title: From local gradient changes to a path-independent integral
passages.caption: Exact segment endpoint changes telescope to ψ(B)−ψ(A) on either path. The finite left-endpoint gradient sum approaches that difference as N increases. Compare the direct and two-leg paths in this global smooth field.

source.text: Along a small segment, the component of ∇ψ in the segment direction gives the local rate of change of ψ. Add the changes over consecutive segments: intermediate endpoint values cancel, leaving only ψ(B)−ψ(A). The finite left-endpoint sum is kept separate from this exact telescoping sum. For the illustrated quadratic field and either available path, the left-endpoint sum differs from ψ(B)−ψ(A) by κ/N degrees C. Its limit is therefore the line integral. Because the endpoint difference is fixed, the integral has the same value for both paths.
source.limit: The illustration uses the globally smooth scalar field ψ=20+2x+y+κ(x²+y²)/2 on all of R², with z fixed and coordinates in metres. The endpoints are fixed at A=(0,0) and B=(1,1). The control N ranges from 1 to 32, κ ranges from 0 to 1.5 degrees C/m², and the path control selects either the direct diagonal or the two-leg path through (1,0). The polynomial and its numerical values are illustrative, not source data. Exact finite telescoping uses segment endpoint changes; only the sampled gradient sum requires a limit. More generally, path independence from a global potential requires an appropriate smooth domain and admissible paths and spanning surfaces.

passages.title: Heat balance in a source-free volume
passages.caption: For the source-free fixed cube, the net outward heat rate is α times its volume. Positive outward flow reduces stored energy; negative outward flow increases it.

source.text: After the initial heating, no further heat energy is generated or absorbed. The outward heat rate is the surface integral of h·n. For the authored cube, it is α times the volume, α*h^3. Conservation therefore gives dQ/dt=-α*h^3 and the local relation dq/dt=-α. Thus, positive net outward flux makes the heat content decrease. An illustrative energy density is q(t)=q0-α*t over a bounded interval for which the initial energy remains positive.
source.limit: The cube is fixed and contains no heat source or sink. Q is total heat energy in joules, and q is energy per volume in joules per cubic metre. The vector h is heat flux in watts per square metre; box side h is a separate scalar label. This concept shows only the sign and the integral and local conservation relations. It does not specify a temperature field or a heat-conduction law. A generic vector flux does not automatically represent a change in stored energy.

passages.title: Cancellation of flux across an internal boundary
passages.caption: A closed volume is divided into two neighboring volumes. Their shared face has opposite outward normals, so its two flux contributions cancel when the cell fluxes are added.

source.text: Let the original closed surface be divided by an internal face. Each new volume includes part of the original outer surface and one copy of the shared face. On that face, the outward normal of one volume is the negative of the outward normal of the other. The vector field is the same at each shared point, so the two normal-flux integrals are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign. After they cancel, the sum of the two cell fluxes contains only the flux through the original outer surface. The same reasoning applies after further subdivisions. In the illustrative affine model, two boxes form a centered cube of side h, with a cut at x=(f−0.5)h. For C=(1+lambda x−omega y, 0.5+omega x+lambda y, 0.25+lambda z), the summed cell flux and the outer flux are both 3lambda h³. The cancellation depends on the opposite normals, not on the position of the cut.
source.limit: The source argument applies to any vector field for which the stated surface integrals exist. The displayed finite calculation is an illustrative affine example, not the source's general proof. The controls use h for cube side, lambda for expansion, omega for rotation, and f for the relative cut position. Both cells use their own outward normal on the shared face. The geometry is two neighboring boxes forming one cube. It does not represent heat conservation, planar-loop circulation, an arbitrary curved-boundary construction, or the later local cube derivation.

passages.title: Heat balance in a source-free cube
passages.caption: Outward heat flow reduces the heat stored in the fixed cube.

source.ref: Section 3-4, printed page 3-6; Eqs. (3.19)–(3.22), with comparison to Eq. (3.13).
source.text: Consider a fixed cube with box side h and no internal heat source. Let q be heat per unit volume, Q the total heat, and h the heat-flow vector. The outward heat rate is the surface flux of h. For a small cube, it is (∇·h)ΔV. The heat inside is qΔV, so its rate of loss is −(∂q/∂t)ΔV. Equating outward flow and loss gives ∂q/∂t = −∇·h. In the authored example h=(αx,0,0), the divergence is α. Therefore, a cube of volume h³ has outward heat rate αh³, dQ/dt=−αh³, and ∂q/∂t=−α. The consistent illustrative density q(t)=q₀−αt is used only over a bounded time for which the stored energy stays positive. For a larger fixed volume, the divergence theorem converts the volume integral of ∇·h into the outward surface flux and gives the same total balance.
source.limit: The cube is fixed and source-free. The authored instantaneous field is h=(αx,0,0) W/m², where α varies from −1 to 1 W/m³ and the box side h varies from 0.2 to 1.2 m. The default values h=1 m and α=0.5 W/m³ are illustrative. A positive α represents net outward flow and decreasing stored heat; a negative α represents net inward flow and increasing stored heat. This model states conservation only. It does not specify Fourier conduction, temperature, conductivity, or a material calibration.

passages.title: Radial heat flow from a point source
passages.caption: A sphere of radius R surrounds a point source in a large block of material. The heat vector h is radially outward and has the same magnitude at all points on the sphere.

source.text: Let W represent the energy liberated per second at the point source. After heat generation has continued for a long time, the temperature is no longer changing anywhere, and the flow is steady. All the heat generated at the source must pass through every closed surface that encloses it. Choose a sphere of radius R centered at the source. For radial, spherically symmetric flow, h is normal to the sphere and constant in magnitude over its area, 4πR². Therefore, ∫S h·n da = h·4πR² = W, so h = W/(4πR²), or h = [W/(4πR²)]e_r. Thus, the same heat rate W crosses every centered sphere, while the heat-flux density varies inversely as the square of the distance from the source.

passages.title: The circulation of a vector field
passages.caption: The signed tangential components of C are integrated all the way around a directed closed loop Γ.

source.ref: Section 3-5, “The circulation of a vector field”; Eq. (3.30); Fig. 3-7; printed page 3-8.
source.text: For any vector field C, take its component along the curved line and integrate this component all the way around the complete loop. The circulation is ∮Γ C_t ds = ∮Γ C · ds. The directed traversal determines the signs of the tangential contributions. The interactive circle is an original bounded example: C=(1+lambda*x-omega*y, 0.5+omega*x+lambda*y, 0.25+lambda*z), and its signed circulation is 2*omega*pi*R^2 for counterclockwise traversal and its negative for clockwise traversal. Lambda and the constant offsets affect the displayed field arrows but have zero full-loop contribution. The arrows show the vector field and the directed path; they do not show material motion.

passages.title: Cancellation on the shared edge of two loops
passages.caption: Two neighboring counterclockwise rectangles form one square boundary. The common edge is traversed upward by the left loop and downward by the right loop. Its two line-integral contributions are equal and opposite, so only the outer boundary remains.

source.text: Divide the original loop into two partial loops by adding a short cut between two boundary points. Use the same sense of rotation for both partial loops. The short cut is then followed in opposite directions, so its contributions have opposite signs and cancel when the two circulations are added. Thus, the sum of the partial-loop circulations equals the circulation around the original outer loop. In the illustrative affine field, the exact combined circulation is 2 omega h² W/m; lambda changes the field expansion but not this circulation.

passages.title: Curl-free fields, path independence, and potential
passages.caption: Compare the direct diagonal path from A to B with the path through (1,0). For the globally smooth authored potential ψ, both exact line integrals equal the same endpoint difference. The finite left-endpoint sum approaches that value as N increases.

source.text: The source starts with a vector field whose curl is zero everywhere. Stokes’ theorem then makes the circulation around an admissible closed loop zero. Two paths between the same endpoints form such a loop, so their line integrals are equal. The integral therefore depends only on the endpoints and can be written as the difference of a scalar potential; the vector field is the gradient of that potential. The visualization uses the authored example ψ=20+2x+y+κ(x²+y²)/2 on all of R², with A=(0,0) and B=(1,1). Its exact endpoint difference is 3+κ. Exact segment endpoint changes telescope for every N on either path. A finite left-endpoint sampled gradient-dot-chord sum is smaller by κ/N for both displayed paths and converges to the integral as N increases.

It is globally smooth on R², so the displayed loops have admissible spanning surfaces within the field domain. passages.title: The curl of a gradient is zero
passages.caption: For the smooth illustrative field ψ=20+2x+y+ηxy, η controls the spatial variation of the gradient, but its curl is zero because the two mixed-derivative terms cancel.

source.ref: Theorem 1, Eq. (3.8); Stokes’ theorem; Section 2-7 vector-algebra result.
source.text: Take the gradient of a smooth scalar field ψ. Its line integral between two points equals ψ at the endpoint minus ψ at the starting point. Around a closed loop, the endpoints are the same, so the integral is zero. Stokes’ theorem then makes the surface integral of ∇×(∇ψ) zero over every spanning surface. Because this holds for every surface, the integrand is zero pointwise: ∇×(∇ψ)=0. In the illustration, ∇ψ=(2+ηy,1+ηx), and the curl is η−η=0.
source.limit: The scalar field is sufficiently smooth for its gradient, curl, and equal mixed partial derivatives to exist. The displayed polynomial is an illustrative example, not source numerical data. The conclusion uses zero circulation around every closed loop and the corresponding Stokes surface argument; one zero loop alone does not establish zero curl everywhere.

passages.title: Closing a surface as its boundary loop shrinks
passages.caption: A sphere of radius R with a dashed north cap removed. The remaining surface has a clockwise boundary when viewed from +z. As the cap angle α approaches zero, the boundary circulation and the curl flux both approach zero on a fixed graph scale.

source.text: The source fills a small loop Γ with a large surface S and then shrinks the loop to a point. If C is finite, the line integral around Γ approaches zero because it is roughly proportional to the shrinking circumference. Stokes’ theorem makes the compatible surface integral of curl C approach the same limit. In this bounded illustration, C=ω(-y,x,0)/2 W/m² and curl C=(0,0,ω) W/m³. For a sphere of radius R with its north cap removed, the clockwise boundary circulation and the curl flux through the remaining outward-oriented surface are both -ωπR² sin²(α) W/m. They vanish analytically as α approaches zero. The completed closed surface therefore has zero total curl flux, matching Eq. (3.39).

passages.title: The divergence of a curl is zero
passages.caption: For the smooth authored field C=(0,0,ηxy), its curl is (ηx,−ηy,0). The divergence cancels between the x and y derivatives. Gauss’ theorem connects this local identity to zero closed-surface flux.

source.text: Apply Gauss’ theorem to ∇ × C: the closed-surface integral of its normal component equals ∫∇ · (∇ × C) dV. The source concludes that this volume integral is zero for any volume. Therefore, for a sufficiently smooth vector field C, ∇ · (∇ × C) = 0 at every point. In the example C = (0, 0, ηxy), the curl is (ηx, −ηy, 0), which can be nonzero, while its divergence is η − η + 0 = 0. For the unit cube, the x-face pair contributes η W/m and the y-face pair contributes −η W/m. Cancellation is between these axis-pair totals; for nonzero η, opposite individual faces do not cancel.

Coulomb’s inverse-square law therefore gives E₂/E₁ = (Δq₂/r₂²)/(Δq₁/r₁²) = 1. The two fields point in opposite directions, so they cancel exactly. All parts of the surface can be paired off in the same way.

Reversing the path also reverses the compatible normal and the signs of both integrals. Changing λ changes the expansion of the field but not its circulation. The source obtains the local square result by a first-order approximation for an infinitesimal square, then sums such squares to state Stokes’ theorem: the boundary circulation equals the surface integral of curl dotted with the compatible normal. The authored affine model gives an exact finite-square equality because midpoint evaluation is exact on every straight edge. Signed directional coefficients do not guarantee that an individual edge integral stays positive or negative throughout the control range.
source.limit: The square is fixed, planar, centered in the xy-plane, and has side h from 0.2 m to 1.2 m. The displayed controls λ and ω range from −1 to 1 W/m³. The orientation control couples counterclockwise traversal with +z and clockwise traversal with −z. Field arrows show only xy components and do not represent material flow. The finite exact result applies to this authored affine field and square; the source’s general local derivation concerns an infinitesimal square. The visualization does not construct an arbitrary curved surface or prove the curl-free and potential results of the next section.

passages.title: One dataset, several copies
passages.caption: Explore the three replication arrangements.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: Replication moves copies of application data between machines. A design must decide where writes enter, how copies receive changes, and which copy serves a read. Availability, read capacity, and proximity to users are motivations; agreement during failure is a separate problem.
source.limit: This map introduces the chapter. It does not model timing, consensus, transactions, or every replication guarantee.

passages.title: One leader orders the write stream
passages.caption: Move one write from the client to the replicas.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: The leader accepts the write and establishes its order in the log. Followers apply that stream. A follower that has not received the write can serve an older value. Replication mechanisms differ, but this experiment uses one ordered synthetic log.
source.limit: One leader, one key, and no failure or concurrent writer. Statement-based, WAL, logical, and trigger replication are outside this aid.

passages.title: When is a write acknowledged?
passages.caption: Compare an asynchronous reply with waiting for follower A.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: An asynchronous reply can reach the client while followers still have an older version. Waiting for a designated follower adds an acknowledgment dependency. If that follower cannot respond, the synchronous write cannot complete under this policy. Another follower may still lag.
source.limit: Only follower A is required in synchronous mode. No claim of universal durability, automatic failover, or acknowledgment by every replica.

passages.title: A snapshot needs a log position
passages.caption: Build a new follower without losing the intervening update.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: Take a consistent snapshot and record its matching log position. Load the snapshot, then replay changes after that position. In the fixture, the snapshot contains version 1 and a later log entry produces version 2. A snapshot alone would leave the new follower behind.
source.limit: The snapshot is already consistent. The experiment omits database-specific backup APIs and snapshot isolation internals.

passages.title: An acknowledged write can be missing after failover
passages.caption: Follow an unreplicated write through leader failure.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: The old leader acknowledges version 2 before its followers receive it. The leader fails and a follower with version 1 is promoted. A subsequent read from the new leader can return version 1. Acknowledgment and survival through this failover are different properties.
source.limit: A selected asynchronous failure trace. Election algorithms, fencing, split brain, and failure detectors are not simulated.

passages.title: Route a read after your own write
passages.caption: Compare a stale follower, the leader, and a minimum-version guard.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: After writing version 2, a client can read version 1 from a lagging follower. Reading the leader can expose the new write in this fixture. A minimum-version guard instead refuses to return a replica state older than the client requires; the client waits or routes elsewhere.
source.limit: One client and one key. The guard is an illustrative strategy, not a database implementation or a linearizability claim.

passages.title: A session must not move backward
passages.caption: Compare new→old, stale→stale, and new→new.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: Monotonic reads constrain the order of states observed by a client. Returning version 2 and then version 1 violates the guarantee. Returning version 1 twice is consistently stale and remains monotonic. Monotonicity alone does not make a read current.
source.limit: One ordered history, one key, and one client session. No global ordering or freshest-read guarantee.

passages.title: A dependent event needs its predecessor
passages.caption: Compare an answer without its question with a valid prefix.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: The synthetic question event precedes and causes the answer. If independent replication streams expose the answer first, the observer sees an order that contradicts this dependency. Seeing neither event, or seeing the question followed by the answer, is compatible with this prefix.
source.limit: One declared causal dependency across two streams. The experiment does not implement a causal tracker, total order, or transaction.

passages.title: Two local successes can conflict
passages.caption: Exchange edits made from the same starting value.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: Two leaders accept different changes to the same key before they exchange updates. Local acceptance does not resolve which result the application should keep. The fixture retains both values as siblings, then shows an explicit application merge.
source.limit: The final merge is an authored example. It is not an automatic CRDT, last-write-wins rule, or general conflict-resolution algorithm.

passages.title: A read can repair a stale replica
passages.caption: Bring an old copy forward using a newer read response.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: Two replicas receive version 2 while a third is offline. A later read compares an up-to-date response with the recovered replica’s version 1. With this single-writer history, the newer version can be returned and written back to repair the old copy. Data that is never read may need anti-entropy.
source.limit: A single ordered write history. Concurrent siblings, clock-based conflict detection, and background anti-entropy are not implemented.

passages.title: Overlap after a completed write
passages.caption: Change write count, read count, and read placement.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: With a fixed set of five replicas, a completed write reaches W members and a read queries R members. W + R > 5 forces overlap between those sets. At equality or below, a read set can miss the write. The result requires the stated membership and completed-write assumptions.
source.limit: Exactly five home replicas, one completed write, no concurrent writes, no failed partial write, no sloppy quorum, and a version order that identifies the fixture’s newer value. Overlap alone does not establish linearizability.

passages.title: Fallback nodes change the overlap argument
passages.caption: Compare a write to fallback nodes with reads from the home set.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: The key normally belongs to three home replicas. During a partition, two fallback replicas accept the write. A read from two home replicas can still miss it even though W + R exceeds the home-set size. Hinted handoff later transfers the held value toward its home replicas.
source.limit: One synthetic partition and handoff. This demonstrates why the fixed-membership proof does not apply; it does not model a full Dynamo system.

passages.title: Concurrent versions are not a single sequence
passages.caption: Compare two independent updates with a later dominating version.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: A version vector records components associated with replicas. Neither [1,0] nor [0,1] dominates the other, so the fixture retains both as concurrent siblings. [1,1] includes both histories in this simplified comparison. Choosing or merging the values remains an application decision.
source.limit: A two-component partial-order illustration. It omits dotted version vectors, pruning, deletes, and the details of a production causal context.

passages.title: Choose a replication design by its tradeoffs
passages.caption: Compare where writes enter and what remains difficult.

source.ref: DDIA · Chapter 5 · sixth early release, July 11, 2016
source.text: Single-leader replication centralizes write ordering but followers may lag. Multiple leaders allow local writes but require conflict handling. Leaderless designs use response sets and version reconciliation. Each arrangement must also handle failures and the guarantees expected by readers.
source.limit: Chapter map, not a performance benchmark or a complete comparison of database products. The labs omit log implementations, replication topologies, transaction-based lag solutions, and full concurrency algorithms.
